items.prompt: Which question does authentication answer?
choices: What may you do?
Who are you?
How fast are you?
Where are you?
items.explanation: Authentication establishes identity. What you may do is authorization.

items.prompt: Which question does authorization answer?
choices: What may you do?
Who are you?
Why are you here?
When did you join?
items.explanation: Authorization decides which actions and data an identified user may touch.

items.prompt: A visitor enters the correct password and is let in. Which step just happened?
choices: Authorization
Compression
Salting
Authentication
items.explanation: Checking a password proves who someone is, which is authentication.

items.prompt: A site checks whether the logged-in user may open the billing page. What is that check called?
choices: Authentication
Hashing
Authorization
Rendering
items.explanation: Deciding what an already-identified user may open is authorization.

items.prompt: A hotel key card opens only your own room. Which part is the authorization?
choices: Showing your ID at the front desk
The card opens only your own room
The colour printed on the card
The name of the hotel
items.explanation: Identity was checked at the desk; limiting the card to one room is the permission.

items.prompt: Showing a passport at a border desk is closest to which idea?
choices: Authentication
Authorization
Hashing
Caching
items.explanation: A passport proves identity. What you may then do in the country is a separate decision.

items.prompt: Can a site have strong authentication and weak authorization?
choices: No, one always implies the other
Only on mobile apps
Only when it uses HTTPS
Yes, they are two separate checks
items.explanation: Proving identity says nothing about permissions, so one can be strong while the other is missing.

items.prompt: Which is an authorization failure?
choices: A wrong password is accepted as correct
A password is stored as plain text
A logged-in customer opens another customer's order page
A login page that loads very slowly for users on mobile networks
items.explanation: The user is who they say they are; the failure is that they were allowed to see someone else's data.

items.prompt: A login page rejects every wrong password correctly, yet any logged-in user can open the /admin URL directly. What is missing?
choices: A stronger hash for the stored passwords on login
A check on each request of what this user may access
A second login factor required on the login form for every visit
Encryption of the admin page address in links
items.explanation: The login check works. Nothing asks whether this identified user is permitted to see /admin.
items.reference:
Two checks, two questions
authentication: who are you? (password, key, fingerprint)
authorization: what may you do? (roles, ownership, rules)
authenticated is not the same as allowed
Why: login proves identity once; every action still needs its own permission check.
items.learnMore:
Authentication versus authorization

Authentication is the front door lock; authorization is which rooms your key opens once inside. Mixing them is a common source of real bugs: an endpoint that checks you are logged in, but never checks that the thing you asked for belongs to you.

Common mistake

Assuming a hidden URL or a required login is enough. Each request needs its own permission check.
items.reflection: Think of a building you enter with a badge. Where is the identity check, and where are the permission checks, and could one exist without the other?

items.prompt: A teammate says: users must log in to reach the API, so per-resource permission checks are unnecessary. What is wrong with that?
choices: Being logged in proves who someone is, not what they may access
Logging in is too slow to be a reliable gate for every single request
Login checks only work for browser-based clients
API requests cannot carry any identity information
items.explanation: Authentication and authorization answer different questions; the first never answers the second.

items.prompt: Which bug is an authorization bug rather than an authentication bug?
choices: A password reset link that never expires after use
A login form accepting an empty password as valid
A session token sent over an unprotected connection
A user changes an invoice number in the URL and sees someone else's invoice
items.explanation: The other three are about proving identity or protecting credentials; this one is about missing permission checks on data.

items.prompt: After confirming a token is valid, an API returns the invoices for whatever user ID the request body contains. What is broken?
choices: The token should be re-hashed on every call
The invoices should be encrypted with the user ID before sending
It should take the user from the verified token, not the request
The user ID should be longer so it is harder to guess
items.explanation: A valid token identifies one user. Trusting an ID the client supplies lets anyone ask for another user's data.

items.prompt: Which is NOT one of the three classic factor categories?
choices: Something you know
Something you post
Something you have
Something you are
items.explanation: The three categories are know, have and are.

items.prompt: A fingerprint scan belongs to which factor category?
choices: Something you are
Something you know
Something you have
Something you lost
items.explanation: Biometrics are traits of the person.

items.prompt: A phone that receives a one-time code belongs to which category?
choices: Something you know
Something you are
Something you share
Something you have
items.explanation: The code proves you possess the registered device.

items.prompt: A password belongs to which factor category?
choices: Something you have
Something you are
Something you know
Something you wear
items.explanation: A password is a secret held in memory.

items.prompt: A hardware security key plugged into a USB port is which category?
choices: Something you know
Something you have
Something you are
Something you read
items.explanation: It is a physical object that you possess.

items.prompt: Which login is multi-factor?
choices: Password plus a code from your phone app
Password plus a security question about your first school
Two different passwords
A PIN plus a longer PIN
items.explanation: Know plus have are two categories. The others stay within one.

items.prompt: Password plus a mother's-maiden-name question counts as how many factors?
choices: Two, because there are two prompts
Three, because both are secrets
Zero, because neither is a device
One, both are things you know
items.explanation: Factors are counted by category, not by number of prompts.

items.prompt: Why do sites ask for a second factor?
choices: It makes the login page load faster
It lets users reuse the same password
Stealing one kind of proof is not enough
It removes the need for passwords entirely
items.explanation: An attacker needs to defeat two different kinds of proof.

items.prompt: A bank asks for a password and then a PIN, both typed from memory. Is that multi-factor authentication?
choices: Yes, because two separate secrets are each checked by the system
No, both are things you know, so it is one factor category
Yes, because the PIN is shorter and harder to guess
No, because a PIN is not a real authentication method
items.explanation: Multi-factor means different categories. Two memorized secrets are still one category.
items.reference:
Count categories, not prompts
🧠 know: password, PIN, answer
📱 have: phone, hardware key
👆 are: fingerprint, face
two knows = still one factor
Why: a second factor only helps if it is a different kind of thing for the attacker to steal.
items.learnMore:
Multi-factor authentication

Each category fails in a different way: secrets leak, devices get lost, traits are hard to change. Combining categories means one theft is no longer enough.

Common mistake

Counting prompts instead of categories. A password and a security question are both knowledge, so they are one factor.
items.reflection: Where in daily life do you rely on two different kinds of proof at once (for example a card and a PIN), and what does each protect against?

items.prompt: An attacker steals a user's password from a leaked file. Which setup still blocks the login?
choices: Password plus a code generated on the user's own phone
Password plus the user's date of birth already held on file
A longer password with symbols the user chose
Password plus a favourite colour security question
items.explanation: The attacker does not have the phone. The other options add only more things that can be known or guessed.

📱 have: phone, hardware key
👆 are: fingerprint, face
two knows = still one factor

items.prompt: A team replaces SMS codes with face unlock on a phone that is also used to receive the login. Which factor categories are now in play for a login on that phone?
choices: Only knowledge, because the phone stores the secret
Only possession, because faces can be photographed
Knowledge and possession, since a face is memorized
Possession of the phone and a trait of the person
items.explanation: The device is something you have; the face is something you are. They are different categories.

items.prompt: Why can two factors from different categories still fail together?
choices: Different categories cancel each other's protection
A second factor is never checked by the server
One attack, such as a fake login page, can capture both at once
Only factors from the same category can be phished
items.explanation: Categories reduce independent theft, but a live attacker relaying both values defeats weak implementations.

items.prompt: Why store a password as a hash instead of plain text?
choices: Hashes make the login page load noticeably faster for users
A stolen file does not reveal readable passwords
Hashes let support read passwords
Hashes are shorter to type
items.explanation: A hash is a one-way fingerprint, so the file alone gives no readable password.

items.prompt: What does a login need to do with a stored password?
choices: Check it, never get it back
Read it aloud to the user
Email it to the user whenever they forget it
Show it to support staff
items.explanation: A check can be done by comparing fingerprints. Recovery is never needed.

items.prompt: Which transformation can be reversed by someone holding the key?
choices: Hashing
Fingerprinting
Salting a hash
Encryption
items.explanation: Encryption is designed to be undone with the key. Hashing is not.

items.prompt: A hash is best described as
choices: A locked box with a spare key
A copy of the input in code
A one-way fingerprint of the input
A shortened password for display
items.explanation: There is no key that turns it back into the original.

items.prompt: A thief steals a file of plain-text passwords. How many accounts are exposed?
choices: Only the newest accounts
Every account in the file
Only accounts with weak passwords
None, the file is useless alone
items.explanation: Plain text means every password is readable immediately.

items.prompt: How does a login check a hashed password?
choices: Hash the typed password and compare the two hashes
Decrypt the stored hash and then compare the plain texts
Email the stored hash to the user
Ask the user to type the hash
items.explanation: Same input gives the same fingerprint, so comparing fingerprints is enough.

items.prompt: Company C encrypts passwords so support can look them up. What is the problem?
choices: Encrypted data cannot be stored in a database
Support staff cannot read encrypted text at all
Encryption makes every login fail
Anyone who gets the key can read every password
items.explanation: If support can recover passwords, so can an attacker who obtains the same key.

items.prompt: Which storage choice leaves a thief with no directly readable password?
choices: Plain text
Reversible encryption
A salted hash
Base64 encoding
items.explanation: Plain text, encryption with a stolen key and Base64 are all reversible.

items.prompt: Two companies lose identical copies of their user database. One stored plain-text passwords, the other stored salted hashes. What is the key difference for the thief?
choices: The plain-text file is harder to copy than the hashed one
The salted hashes cannot simply be read back as passwords
Both reveal the same passwords but at different speeds
The hashed file always contains fewer user accounts
items.explanation: The stored form decides what the thief can read. A hash must be guessed against; plain text just reads.
items.reference:
What can the thief do with the file?
🔓 plain text: read every password
🔑 encrypted: read all, once the key is also stolen
🔒 hashed: must guess and check, nothing to read
Why: a login only checks a password, so store a one-way fingerprint that cannot be turned back.
items.learnMore:
Hashing versus encryption

Encryption is for data you need back, a message or a file. A password is only ever compared, so the right tool is a one-way hash with no key to steal.

Common mistake

Reasoning that encrypting is stronger than hashing. For passwords, being reversible is the weakness.
items.reflection: Think of something you keep only to check against later, such as a receipt number. What would you lose if you kept the original instead of just a way to verify it?

items.prompt: A teammate proposes: encrypt the password column, since we already have key management. What does an attacker gain that hashing would have denied?
choices: A way to recover every real password once the key is obtained
A faster way to check whether many users have reused one password
Permission to bypass the login page entirely
Access to the hashes of other users' sessions
items.explanation: Encryption is reversible by design. If the key leaks with the data, the passwords are plain text again.

items.prompt: Why is it acceptable that a hashed password can never be shown back to the user on request?
choices: Users forget passwords too often to be shown them again on request
Hashes are too long to display on a screen
Retrieval is possible but is disabled by default
The system only ever needs to check passwords, not retrieve them
items.explanation: Verification compares fingerprints, so recovery is unnecessary. A forgotten password is replaced, not revealed.

items.prompt: A site stores each password as Base64 of its text. Why is this no better than plain text?
choices: Base64 produces output strings that are too short to be unique for each user
Base64 is slower than any real hash function
Base64 is a reversible encoding with no key, so anyone can undo it
Base64 strings cannot be stored in text fields
items.explanation: Encoding is not protection. A one-way function with no way back is what stops reading.

items.prompt: After a successful login, what does the browser usually send on later requests?
choices: The password again
A session ID or token
The stored hash
The random salt
items.explanation: The token stands in for the proof of identity given at login.

items.prompt: Why not check the password on every single request?
choices: It is slow and spreads the password everywhere
Passwords expire after one request
Servers cannot hash more than once
Browsers refuse to send the same password twice in a row
items.explanation: One check at login, then a short-lived credential, keeps the password in as few places as possible.

items.prompt: In the wristband picture, what is the wristband?
choices: The password
The salt
The stored hash
The session ID or token
items.explanation: It says this visitor already proved identity.

items.prompt: How often is the password involved in the chain?
choices: On every request
Only at logout
Once, at login
Only after expiry
items.explanation: After login, the token does the work.

items.prompt: A server revokes a token. What does that mean?
choices: It becomes valid for longer
It stops working before its normal expiry
It is copied into the main user database table
It is converted into a password
items.explanation: Revoked means invalidated early by the server.

items.prompt: Who can use a stolen, still-valid token?
choices: Whoever presents it
Only the original user
Only users on the same device
Nobody, tokens cannot be reused
items.explanation: The server cannot tell the thief from the user if the token is valid.

items.prompt: What does password hashing protect?
choices: A token while it is in transit
A cookie in a user's browser
The web address of the login page
The stored copy of the password
items.explanation: Hashing applies to the saved password record, not to tokens.

items.prompt: Where should a session token never travel unprotected?
choices: Inside an HTTPS connection
Between the server and its own database
Over plain HTTP
Inside a locked cookie jar
items.explanation: Plain HTTP can be read by anyone on the path, which is why transport protection matters.

items.prompt: An attacker never learns a user's password but copies the user's valid token from an unprotected network. Does careful password hashing help now?
choices: Yes, the token is only valid for hashed accounts
No, hashing protects the stored password, not a token in use
Yes, the server rehashes the token on each request
No, because the token is simply the stored hash of the user's password
items.explanation: Once logged in, the server looks at the token only. Whoever holds it is treated as the user.
items.reference:
The chain, left to right
1. password → hash check (once)
2. server issues a token (the wristband)
3. every later request shows the token
4. server validates the token, not the password
Why: two different secrets, two different places to protect them.
items.learnMore:
From proof to wristband

A login is expensive and exposes the password, so the server exchanges it for a short-lived credential. That credential then becomes the thing worth stealing.

Common mistake

Treating password storage as the whole of authentication. The token needs expiry, revocation and safe transport too.
items.reflection: Where else does a one-time check hand you a temporary pass that is then shown repeatedly (an event wristband, a visitor badge)? What happens if someone copies the pass?

items.prompt: Why is protecting the token a separate problem from protecting the password?
choices: After login the token is what the server accepts as proof
Tokens are chosen by the user in the same way that passwords are
Tokens are stored in the password database
Tokens expire before passwords are ever hashed
items.explanation: Each credential has its own places to leak, so each needs its own defence.

2. server issues a token (the wristband)
3. every later request shows the token
4. server validates the token, not the password
Why: two different secrets, two different places to protect them.

items.prompt: A user changes their password, but an old session still works on another device. What does this show?
choices: The new password was not hashed correctly
The old password is still stored in plain text
Tokens are recomputed from the current password on each request made
Sessions outlive the password check and need their own revocation
items.explanation: The password is only checked at login. Existing tokens keep working unless the server revokes them.

items.prompt: At which point in the chain does the server compare hashes?
choices: On every single request that carries a valid session token
When the token expires on its own
At login only, when the password is submitted
Whenever the browser reloads a page
items.explanation: Later requests are validated by token. The password hash is touched only at login.

2. server issues a token (the wristband)
3. every later request shows the token
4. server validates the token, not the password

items.prompt: What is a salt?
choices: A second password the user types at every login
A random value mixed in before hashing
A key that decrypts the hash
A compressed copy of the password
items.explanation: It makes the same password produce a different hash for each user.

items.prompt: Where is a user's salt usually stored?
choices: Right next to their hash
Only in the user's browser
In a separate secret vault only
Inside the password itself
items.explanation: The server needs it at every login, and it is not a secret.

items.prompt: Two users have the same password and different salts. Their hashes are
choices: Identical
Always empty
The same length as the salt
Different
items.explanation: Different salts give different inputs to the hash.

items.prompt: Two users have the same password and no salt. Their hashes are
choices: Different
Encrypted
Identical
Missing
items.explanation: Same input, same fingerprint.

items.prompt: What is a rainbow table?
choices: A table of users sorted by signup date and then by country
A precomputed list of common passwords and their hashes
A list of all stored salts
A chart of login times
items.explanation: It trades one big upfront computation for instant lookups later.

items.prompt: What defeats a precomputed table?
choices: A unique salt for every user
A longer username
Using HTTPS on the login page
Asking users to log in twice
items.explanation: The table would have to be rebuilt for each salt.

items.prompt: Does the salt have to be kept secret?
choices: Yes, as secret as the password
Yes, secret from the server too
No, it can be identical for all
No, it only has to be unique
items.explanation: Its job is uniqueness, not secrecy.

items.prompt: At login, which salt does the server mix in?
choices: A new random one each time
The one from the first user
The one stored for that user
None, only the password
items.explanation: It must reproduce the same hash it made at registration.

items.prompt: A team mixes the same fixed salt into every password before hashing. Does this stop a rainbow table?
choices: Yes, any salt at all fully stops precomputation
Only generic ones, an attacker builds one table for that salt
No, a fixed salt makes every hash identical to the unsalted version
Yes, because the fixed salt is a secret key
items.explanation: A single shared salt means a single new table cracks every user with a common password.
items.reference:
Same password, two users
no salt: hash A = hash A → one lookup cracks both
shared salt: still identical → one new table cracks all
unique salt: hash A ≠ hash B → work repeated per user
Why: salting does not slow one guess, it stops the work from being shared.
items.learnMore:
Salting and rainbow tables

A rainbow table is saved work. A unique random salt per user makes saved work worthless, because every user has their own version of the problem.

Common mistake

Thinking a single secret salt baked into the code is as good as one per user. Shared means shareable.
items.reflection: Think of a lock that ships with the same key for every house. How does giving each house its own key change what a thief's one copy is worth?

items.prompt: An attacker steals the file and sees every salt in plain view. Has salting failed?
choices: No, it still forces separate guessing work for each user
Yes, because a visible salt can simply be subtracted from the hash
Yes, salts only work while kept secret
No, because salts are never stored in the file
items.explanation: Salts are stored with the hash by design. Their value is uniqueness, not secrecy.
items.reference:
Same password, two users
no salt: hash A = hash A → one lookup cracks both
shared salt: still identical → one new table cracks all
unique salt: hash A ≠ hash B → work repeated per user
Why: salting does not slow one guess, it stops the work from being shared.
items.learnMore:
Salting and rainbow tables

A rainbow table is saved work. A unique random salt per user makes saved work worthless, because every user has their own version of the problem.

Common mistake

Thinking a single secret salt baked into the code is as good as one per user. Shared means shareable.
items.reflection: Think of a lock that ships with the same key for every house. How does giving each house its own key change what a thief's one copy is worth?

items.prompt: A site generates a fresh random salt at every login attempt and does not store it. What happens?
choices: Logins work and are safer than before
Only users with long passwords are blocked
The stored hash is silently updated on each login attempt made
The correct password never reproduces the stored hash
items.explanation: The login must mix in the same salt used at registration, so the salt must be stored.
items.reference:
Same password, two users
no salt: hash A = hash A → one lookup cracks both
shared salt: still identical → one new table cracks all
unique salt: hash A ≠ hash B → work repeated per user
Why: salting does not slow one guess, it stops the work from being shared.

Crack the shared salt first, which then reveals both passwords
Run the guessing work separately against each of them
Nothing, identical passwords hash to the same value

items.prompt: A one-way hash means the attacker cannot
choices: Guess any password
Run the hash backwards
Read any stored hash from the file
Use a computer
items.explanation: They can still guess and hash each guess.

items.prompt: What can an attacker do with a stolen hash and its salt?
choices: Guess passwords, hash each, and compare
Decrypt it with the salt
Read the password directly from the hash
Log in with the hash itself
items.explanation: Offline guessing is the main remaining attack.

items.prompt: What does a slow key-derivation function do?
choices: Makes logins impossible
Removes the need for salt
Encrypts the password
Makes every single guess take longer
items.explanation: Each guess costs the attacker the same extra time it costs the server at login.

items.prompt: Which of these are password-oriented KDFs?
choices: HTTP, TCP and DNS
JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP formats
bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2
HTML, CSS and SVG
items.explanation: These are designed to be deliberately slow.

items.prompt: In this unit's model, each extra random character multiplies the work by about
items.explanation: There are 94 printable characters per position in the model.

items.prompt: A slower hash means the time to crack becomes
choices: Longer
Shorter
Unchanged
Random
items.explanation: Fewer guesses per second means more seconds in total.

items.prompt: Why is a fast hash a poor choice for storing passwords?
choices: It produces hashes that are too long
It cannot be combined with a salt
It reveals the password to the server
It lets an attacker guess very quickly
items.explanation: Speed that is good for files is bad for passwords.

items.prompt: In the model, how many guesses does the attacker try on average before success?
choices: All of the possible combinations
One quarter of them
Half of all combinations
Exactly one
items.explanation: On average the right answer sits halfway through the search.

items.prompt: In the model, an 8-character random password takes about 35 days at the fast speed. About how long at the slow speed (10^7 times slower)?
choices: About 3,500,000 years
About 966,500 years
About 9,665 years
About 96,650 days
items.explanation: 35 days multiplied by 10^7 is about 3.5 × 10^8 days, roughly 966,500 years.
items.reference:
Two levers that multiply
length: each extra random character × 94
speed: slower hash → fewer guesses per second
8 chars: ~35 days (fast) vs ~966,500 years (slow)
assumed speeds 10^9 and 10^2 per second
Why: total time is combinations divided by guesses per second, so shrinking the rate is as strong as adding length.
items.learnMore:
Why password hashes are slow on purpose

A real login runs the hash once, so a tenth of a second is invisible. An attacker runs it billions of times, so the same delay becomes the whole cost.

Common mistake

Treating one-way as sufficient. A fast one-way function still lets an attacker guess at full speed.
items.reflection: Think of a lock that takes two seconds to open. That is nothing to you once a day. What does it mean to someone who has to try ten million keys?

items.prompt: At the fast speed a 10-character random password takes about 854 years. Roughly how long for a 9-character one?
choices: About 9 years
About 80 years
About 90 days
About 800 years
items.explanation: Removing one character divides the work by 94, so 854 divided by 94 is about 9.

Real attackers can run the hash backwards
Real hash functions are faster than the model assumes
People pick guessable passwords, so far fewer than all combinations are tried first

items.prompt: Which single change helps every user without asking anyone to change their password?
choices: Adding a longer password hint to the login page for each user
Making the salt longer for new users
Switching to a deliberately slow, tunable hash
Shortening the session lifetime
items.explanation: The slowdown applies to all stored passwords, whatever users chose.

items.prompt: Which comparison can leak information through timing?
choices: One that always checks every byte before answering
One that stops at the first differing byte
One that compares only lengths
One that is never used
items.explanation: Early exit makes rejection time depend on how much matched.

items.prompt: A constant-time comparison always
choices: Takes the same time wherever bytes differ
Stops at the very first byte mismatch it finds
Returns true for equal lengths
Skips the comparison
items.explanation: That removes the timing signal.

items.prompt: Why is plain SHA-256 a poor password hash?
choices: It cannot be salted
It is reversible
It produces a short result
It is designed to run very fast
items.explanation: A fast function lets an attacker guess more per second.

items.prompt: One hardcoded salt for every user is
choices: Strong, because the salt is kept secret in code
Required by all KDFs
Weak, one table cracks all common passwords
Harmless if the salt is long
items.explanation: Uniqueness per user is what the salt is for.

items.prompt: Why avoid inventing your own login scheme?
choices: Libraries are always slower to run in production
Small slips silently remove protections
Custom code cannot use salts
Hashes cannot be written by hand
items.explanation: Each piece looks simple, which is what makes mistakes easy.

items.prompt: Which is the safer choice for hashing passwords?
choices: A maintained, audited library
A function you wrote last week
A shorter hash so it is quicker
A single global salt
items.explanation: Audited code has been tested against the known failure modes.

items.prompt: A good reviewer asks how each login piece
choices: Looks in the editor
Names its variables
Formats its output
Fails, not only whether it passes
items.explanation: All four failures pass the happy-path test.

items.prompt: Salting alone makes a fast hash safe. True or false?
choices: True, salts slow every guess
True, salts replace slow hashes
False, guesses still run at full speed
False, salts are reversible
items.explanation: Salting stops sharing, not speed.

items.prompt: A reviewer sees: per-user salt, slow KDF, plain equality on the hash. Which weakness is left, and can it be used without stealing the database?
choices: Shared salt across all users; no, the database must be stolen first
Timing leak from equality; yes, through repeated login attempts
Fast hashing; no, the file is needed
Custom scheme; no, source code is needed
items.explanation: Salt and KDF are fine. Response times through the live login endpoint can leak how much matched.
items.reference:
Four leaks the happy path hides
⚡ fast hash → quick offline guessing
⏱ plain equality → timing signal
🧂 one shared salt → one table cracks all
🛠 homemade scheme → silent slips
Why: each mechanism is simple alone, and each hides a way to fail that normal tests never run.
items.learnMore:
Review for failure, not success

These checks all pass a normal login. A reviewer has to ask what an attacker with a copied file, or a stopwatch, could do with each piece.

Common mistake

Treating a working login as proof of a secure one.
items.reflection: Think of a door that opens for the right key and stays shut for the wrong one. What else would you test before trusting it with something valuable?

items.prompt: A login uses a unique random salt per user and one fast hash pass. The file is stolen. Which failure applies?

Precomputed tables still crack every user at once
The comparison leaks timing to the thief
The salt is exposed, so hashing is undone
items.explanation: Unique salts block shared work, but each single guess is cheap.

items.prompt: Implement `keyspace(alphabet, length)`: how many different passwords exist when each of `length` positions can be any of `alphabet` characters.
items.explanation: Each position multiplies the count by the alphabet size, so the total is alphabet to the power of length.

items.prompt: Implement `averageGuesses(combinations)`: on average the attacker succeeds after trying half of all combinations.
items.explanation: Half the space is searched on average before the right answer comes up.

items.prompt: Implement `secondsToTry(guesses, perSecond)`: how many seconds it takes to make that many guesses at that rate.
items.explanation: Time is total work divided by rate.

items.prompt: Implement `hoursFromSeconds(seconds)`: convert seconds to hours.
items.explanation: An hour is 3600 seconds.

items.prompt: Implement `daysFromSeconds(seconds)`: convert seconds to days.
items.explanation: A day is 24 times 3600, which is 86400 seconds.

items.prompt: Implement `guessesPerSecond(exponent)`: the demo describes speed as 10 to the power x guesses per second. Return that rate.
items.explanation: A speed written as an exponent is ten raised to that exponent.

items.prompt: Implement `digitsKeyspace(length)`: how many PINs of that many digits exist (digits 0 to 9).
items.explanation: Ten choices per position, so ten to the power of the length.

items.prompt: Implement `slowdownFactor(fastRate, slowRate)`: by what factor does the attacker's time grow when the guess rate drops from `fastRate` to `slowRate`?
items.explanation: Time is inversely proportional to the rate, so the ratio of the rates is the ratio of the times.

items.prompt: Implement `averageCrackSeconds(alphabet, length, perSecond)`: the average seconds to find a random password of that length over that alphabet, when the attacker tries guesses at `perSecond` and succeeds on average after half the combinations.
items.explanation: Combinations are alphabet to the power of length, half are tried on average, and dividing by the rate gives seconds.
items.reference:
Average crack time, from the model
combinations = alphabet size to the power of length
average guesses = combinations / 2
seconds = average guesses / guesses per second
slower hash → smaller rate → more seconds
Why: writing the formula once makes every table in this unit reproducible.
items.learnMore:
Turning the model into a function

Each piece is one line of arithmetic: how many combinations exist, half of them on average, divided by how fast guesses run. Writing it is how you check you understand which lever does what.

Common mistake

Forgetting the halving, or dividing by the wrong quantity so a faster hash looks safer.
items.reflection: Pick any lock or code you rely on. Estimate how many combinations it has and how fast someone could try them. Which number surprises you?

items.prompt: Implement `minLengthToExceed(alphabet, perSecond, targetSeconds)`: the smallest password length whose average crack time (half the combinations at `perSecond`) is at least `targetSeconds`.
items.explanation: Start at length 1 and grow it until the average time reaches the target. The comparison must be strictly less to keep going so that exactly meeting the target stops the loop.

Why: writing the formula once makes every table in this unit reproducible.

items.explanation: Compute the average seconds, then compare with the target. Meeting the target exactly counts as safe, so the comparison is greater-or-equal.
